figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of OMD-Bench. All modalities initially depict the same anchor (a dog). We systematically corrupt subsets of modalities, replacing them with different anchor’s content, and evaluate whether models can still answer correctly or appropriately abstain.
Figure 12: E2: False abstention - typewriter (k=0, GPT-4o-Mini, synthetic).
Figure 13: E3: Missed abstention - piano (k=3, Qwen3o-Instruct, real).
Table 7: CoT effect (synthetic). ∆: CoT − ZS. Positive ∆C000 = CoT helps accuracy. Positive ∆ACE = CoT worsens calibration.

Table 8: Abstention Calibration Error (ACE, %, ↓) across all four settings. ACE = 1 4 ∑3 k=0 |Absk − Abs∗k|, where Abs∗k is the human-annotated abstention rate at corruption level k; 0 = perfectly aligned with human abstention behavior. Models sorted by ZS Synthetic ACE.
Figure 8: E1: Wrong factual answer – train (k=0, MiniCPM, synthetic).

Table 1: Accuracy (%) across corruption levels. At k≤1, values reflect factual correctness (higher = better). At k≥2, values reflect the rate of correct response per the human annotation protocol (higher = better). k̄=1,2 averages

Table 2: Abstention rates (%) across corruption levels. The Human row shows evidence-based target rates from our annotation protocol: abstention is near-zero at k≤2 (the remaining clean modalities suffice) and near-universal
Figure 16: E3: Missed abstention - cat (k=3, MiniCPM, synthetic).
Figure 9: E1: Wrong factual answer - car (k=1, Gemini 2.5, synthetic).
Figure 4: Per-condition open-ended accuracy (%) averaged across judges and splits. Rows show each (model, prompt) configuration. White lines separate corruption levels.
Figure 3: Open-ended accuracy by corruption level, split by judge. Each line is a (model, prompt) configuration averaged across both data splits.
Figure 5: E1: Wrong factual answer - piano (k=0, Gemini 2.5, real).
Figure 10: E2: Wrong abstention - horse (k=2, Gemini 2.5, real).
Figure 15: E3: Missed abstention - typewriter (k=3, Qwen3o-Instruct, real).
Table 6: Per-condition accuracy (%, synthetic, zero-shot). Cxyz = corruption vector (cv, ca, ct); 1 = corrupted.
Figure 2: MCQ vs. open-ended accuracy across corruption levels. Shaded area shows the ZS performance gap. MCQ values are from Table 1; open-ended values are averaged across judges and splits.

Table 3: Mean predictive confidence (%) across corruption levels. Persistent high confidence as k increases indicates overconfidence. Models sorted by k=0 confidence (ZS, Synthetic) within each group. M.: confidence extraction method - TP = token probability (full vocabulary); RS = restricted softmax (5 answer options). TP and RS are on different scales and are not directly comparable. Gemini 2.0 and MiniCPM omitted (no token-level data
Figure 6: E1: Wrong factual answer - bubble wrap (k=1, MiniCPM, synthetic).
Table 16: Per-anchor accuracy (%) at k=0 for Gemini 2.5 (synthetic, zero-shot). 22 of 27 anchors are solved perfectly; the five below 100% mainly reflect harder knowledge questions.

Table 15: Abstention Calibration Error (ACE, %, ↓) with 95% bootstrap CIs (synthetic split, 10,000 resamples). CIs confirm that the top two models (Gemini 2.5, Qwen3o-Think) are separated from the bottom cluster (VideoLLaMA2, Phi-4, VITA-1.5) by non-overlapping intervals. Models sorted by ZS ACE.

Table 14: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for modality reliance (synthetic, zero-shot). ∆̄: mean per-anchor accuracy drop difference (positive = text corruption hurts more). Text–audio significance holds for all ten models; text–video for six. ∗p<.05; ∗∗p<.01; ∗∗∗p<.001.
Table 5: Normalized reliance ∆norm m (zero-shot). Higher = more sensitive to that modality’s corruption.

Figure 7: E1: Wrong factual answer - gun (k=1, GPT-4o-Mini, synthetic).

Table 13: Human-annotated abstention distribution across corruption levels (k) and splits. Abstention is near-zero for k ≤ 1, marginal for k=2 except when text and visual are jointly corrupted, and near-universal (≈98%) under full tri-modal corruption (k=3). Cell
